heading: READING PASSAGE 1
instructionBanner: You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 1–13, which are based on Reading Passage 1 below.
title: PASSAGE 1: The Future of Personalised Education
text:
Over the past century, education has evolved considerably. Traditional classrooms, where every student followed the same curriculum at the same pace, were once regarded as the most efficient way to teach large groups. Today, however, advances in educational research and digital technology have encouraged schools and universities to adopt more flexible approaches that recognise the individual needs of learners.

One of the most significant developments has been personalised learning. This approach recognises that students differ in their prior knowledge, learning speed, interests, and preferred methods of studying. Rather than expecting every learner to complete identical activities, personalised education seeks to adapt lessons to suit each individual's strengths while also providing additional support in weaker areas.

Digital technology has accelerated this transformation. Learning management systems, educational applications, and artificial intelligence can now analyse a student's performance almost instantly. When a learner repeatedly struggles with a particular concept, the software can recommend extra exercises, explanatory videos, or simplified examples. Conversely, students who demonstrate rapid understanding can be offered more challenging activities without waiting for the rest of the class.

Research suggests that personalised learning may increase student motivation. Many learners become more engaged when they receive immediate feedback and feel that lessons are relevant to their own abilities. Furthermore, allowing students to progress at an appropriate pace can reduce anxiety, particularly for those who require additional practice before mastering new concepts.

Despite these advantages, personalised education also presents challenges. Teachers must interpret large amounts of learning data and decide how best to respond to each student's progress. This responsibility requires additional training and careful planning. Technology can assist teachers, but it cannot replace professional judgement, empathy, or classroom experience.

Another concern involves educational equality. Schools with limited financial resources may struggle to purchase modern technology or provide reliable internet access. As a result, students from disadvantaged communities may have fewer opportunities to benefit from personalised learning systems than those attending better-funded institutions.

Privacy has become another important issue. Modern educational platforms collect considerable amounts of information about students, including assessment results, learning behaviour, and sometimes even communication records. Schools therefore have a responsibility to ensure that personal data is stored securely and used only for legitimate educational purposes. Many countries have introduced regulations governing how educational institutions collect, store, and process student information.

Experts increasingly argue that successful personalised education depends on achieving an appropriate balance between technology and human interaction. Computers can analyse performance rapidly and identify learning patterns that would be difficult for teachers to detect manually. However, teachers remain essential for encouraging critical thinking, creativity, collaboration, and emotional development—qualities that are not easily measured by software.

Looking ahead, many researchers believe personalised learning will continue to expand as artificial intelligence becomes more sophisticated. Future systems may predict learning difficulties before they occur, recommend individual study plans, and provide highly adaptive educational experiences. Nevertheless, educational specialists generally agree that technology should remain a tool that supports teachers rather than replacing them entirely.
